c: What is under the holes

A solderless breadboard is a plastic block with hundreds of small holes, each sitting above a metal spring clip. Push a component lead or a wire into a hole and the clip grips it. The clips are joined in groups beneath the surface, so two leads pushed into the same group are electrically connected with no solder. Pull a part out and the connection is gone. The name comes from early radio hobbyists who built circuits on wooden boards meant for slicing bread.
The pattern of connections

The main area is divided into short rows of five holes. The five holes in each row are connected to one another and to nothing else. A groove runs down the centre of the board, and rows on opposite sides of the groove are not connected. Along each long edge run one or two strips, usually marked with red and blue lines, connected along their whole length. These are the power rails, intended for the supply voltage and ground.
Why the centre groove exists

The groove is spaced to fit a standard chip in a dual in-line package, the kind with two parallel rows of legs. Place the chip straddling the groove and each leg lands in its own row of five, with four free holes beside it for connections. If you put a chip anywhere else, its legs on one side would be shorted together. Small push buttons are sized to straddle the groove too.
The split rail trap

On many full-size boards, the power rails are broken in the middle, so the left half and right half are separate. There is often a visible gap in the red and blue lines at that point, but not always. Beginners regularly power one end of the board and wonder why chips at the other end are dead. If your board has the break, add a short jumper wire across it on each rail. Check with the continuity beep if unsure.
Wire and parts that fit

Use solid core wire of about 22 gauge, or ready-made jumper leads with pins on the ends. Stranded wire splays and will not go in. Thick leads, such as those on large diodes or screw terminals, can permanently stretch the clips so that they no longer grip thinner wires afterwards. Keep wires short and flat against the board where you can, and use consistent colours, red for the supply and black for ground. Tidy boards are far easier to debug.
What breadboards are bad at

The clips and long metal strips add a small amount of resistance and stray capacitance to every connection. For slow signals and modest currents this does not matter. For fast signals, radio circuits or anything above a few megahertz, it can stop a correct design from working. Currents much above an amp will heat the clips. Breadboards are also unreliable over time, as wires work loose. They are for trying ideas, not for anything you intend to keep.
The usual faults

When a breadboard circuit misbehaves, the cause is usually mechanical. A wire is one row off. A lead is not pushed fully home. A power rail is not connected. A chip is in backwards. Before doubting your design, check that every chip has both power and ground at its pins using a meter, then trace each wire from end to end. Building in small stages and testing after each one makes these errors easy to find.
Moving on from the breadboard

Once a circuit works, there are several ways to make it permanent. Stripboard and perfboard are cheap copper-clad boards you solder parts onto and wire by hand. Some prototype boards copy the breadboard's row layout exactly, so you can transfer a design hole for hole. For anything you want more than one of, a custom printed circuit board, drawn in free software and ordered online, now costs only a few dollars for a small batch.
The right pressure

The correct pressure for your tyres is printed on a sticker inside the driver's door frame, and in the manual. It is not the number moulded into the tyre's sidewall, which is the maximum the tyre can hold. The door figure was chosen by the car maker to balance grip, comfort, wear and fuel economy for that vehicle. Front and rear pressures sometimes differ, and there may be a higher figure for a full load.
Check it cold, monthly

Tyres lose a little air all the time, and pressure also changes with temperature, dropping by roughly one pound per square inch for every 10 degrees Fahrenheit the air cools. Check once a month and before long trips, when the tyres are cold, meaning before driving or after only a short distance. A digital gauge costs very little and is more reliable than the ones on forecourt air lines. Include the spare if the car has one.
What low pressure does

An under-inflated tyre flexes more as it rolls. That builds heat, wears the outer edges of the tread, increases fuel consumption and lengthens stopping distances. In the worst case, heat causes the tyre to fail at speed. The dashboard warning light for tyre pressure generally comes on only when a tyre is about a quarter below the recommended figure. By then it has been low for some time, so the light is a backstop, not a substitute for checking.
Tread depth

Tread grooves exist to channel water out from under the tyre. As they wear shallow, the tyre begins to ride on top of the water in heavy rain and grip disappears. In most of the United States, the legal minimum is two thirty-seconds of an inch. Tyres have small raised bars in the grooves that become level with the tread at that depth. Wet braking deteriorates well before the legal limit, and many safety groups recommend replacing at four thirty-seconds.
The coin test

You can check tread without a gauge. Put an American penny into a groove with Lincoln's head pointing down. If you can see the top of his head, the tread is at or below the legal minimum. Do the same with a quarter. If the top of Washington's head is visible, the tread is below four thirty-seconds and wet grip is reduced. Check several places across each tyre, since uneven wear is common.
What uneven wear means

The pattern of wear is diagnostic. Wear on both outer edges points to under-inflation. Wear down the centre points to over-inflation. Wear on one edge only suggests the wheels are out of alignment. Scalloped or patchy wear can indicate worn suspension parts or an unbalanced wheel. Rotating the tyres between positions at the interval in the manual, typically every 5,000 to 8,000 miles, evens out wear and extends their life.
Reading the sidewall

A marking such as 225/60R17 describes the size. The first number is the width in millimetres. The second is the height of the sidewall as a percentage of the width. R means radial construction, and the last number is the wheel diameter in inches. Elsewhere, after the letters DOT, a four-digit code gives the week and year of manufacture. A tyre marked 2321 was made in the twenty-third week of 2021.
Age matters too

Rubber hardens and cracks with age, whatever the tread depth. Many vehicle and tyre manufacturers recommend replacing tyres somewhere between six and ten years after manufacture, even if they look serviceable. This catches people out on cars that are driven little, and on spares and trailers. Look for fine cracks in the sidewalls and bulges, which indicate internal damage. A bulging tyre should be replaced before the car is driven any distance.
Turn the question around

The nineteenth-century German mathematician Carl Jacobi is said to have advised his students to invert, always invert, when stuck on a hard problem. Mathematicians do this routinely, proving a statement by showing that its opposite leads to a contradiction. The investor Charlie Munger made the idea widely known outside mathematics. His version was that it is often easier to see what will make a venture fail than what will make it succeed, and avoiding the first gets you a long way.
Why backwards is easier

Success usually has many requirements, all of which must be met, and they are hard to list. Failure often needs only one thing to go wrong, and the candidates are easy to name. Asked what makes a good marriage, people offer vague generalities. Asked what would reliably ruin one, they answer at once and specifically: contempt, dishonesty, neglect. The inverted question produces a concrete list of things not to do, and a list of that kind can be acted on.
The bombers

During the Second World War, the American military studied bombers returning from missions to decide where to add armour. The damage was concentrated on the wings and fuselage, so those areas seemed the obvious places. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw. They were looking only at aircraft that had come back. The planes hit in the engines had not returned. Armour belonged where the surviving planes showed no holes. He had asked not where planes get hit, but where hits are fatal.
Avoiding stupidity

A great deal of good performance consists of not making large errors. In amateur tennis, most points are lost through mistakes, not won by brilliant shots, so the amateur who simply keeps the ball in play beats the one going for winners. Investing is similar. Avoiding ruinous losses does more for long-term results than finding spectacular gains. Trying to be consistently not foolish is a more achievable aim than trying to be brilliant, and it often yields better results.
Applying it to a goal

Take any goal and ask how you would guarantee the opposite. To ruin your health: sleep little, never move, eat badly, ignore symptoms. To fail at a job: miss deadlines, hide problems, blame others, stop learning. To lose money: borrow to speculate, put everything in one place, panic and sell at the bottom. Then check your current habits against the list. People are often surprised to find that they are already doing two or three of the items.
For products and plans

Designers and engineers use the same move. Instead of asking what would make the product delightful, ask what would make a customer give up and leave. Instead of asking how the project will succeed, ask what would kill it. Safety engineering is built on this principle. Engineers list every way a system could fail and design against each one. Aviation's safety record comes less from making flights go well than from systematically removing the ways they go badly.
What inversion cannot do

Avoiding failure is not the same as achieving excellence. A life spent only on eliminating mistakes can become timid. Inversion will not give you the idea for a great product or a piece of music. Its role is to clear the ground. It removes the obvious errors and the avoidable disasters so that your effort is not wasted. The positive work of creating something still has to be done by other means.
A five-minute exercise

Choose one goal that matters to you this year. Write at the top of a page: how could I make sure this fails? List everything you can think of for five minutes. Circle the three items you are most at risk of actually doing. Decide on one specific safeguard for each. The page takes less time than most planning meetings and is often more useful, because guarding against known failures is something you can start on today.
A piece of ownership

A share of stock is a unit of ownership in a company. If a firm has issued one million shares and you hold one thousand, you own a thousandth of it: a thousandth of its buildings, its brands, its debts and its future profits. Shareholders elect the board of directors, who appoint the managers. Your liability is limited to what you paid. If the company fails owing billions, creditors cannot come after your house.
Why companies issue shares

Companies sell shares to raise money without borrowing. A business that needs funds to build a factory can take a loan, which must be repaid with interest, or sell part of itself to investors, who share in whatever results. The first sale of shares to the public is an initial public offering. After that, shares change hands between investors on a stock exchange. The company receives nothing from this later trading. It is one investor selling to another.
How shareholders are paid

Owners earn a return in two ways. Some companies distribute part of their profits in cash, called dividends, usually every quarter. Others keep their profits and reinvest them, aiming to make the business more valuable, in which case shareholders benefit if the share price rises. Many do both. A company may also buy back its own shares, which leaves each remaining share with a slightly larger claim on the business.
Price and size

The price of one share says nothing by itself about how big or expensive a company is. A firm with shares at 20 dollars can be far larger than one with shares at 2,000, if it has many more shares outstanding. The figure that matters is market capitalization: share price multiplied by the number of shares. When a company splits each share into several, the price falls in proportion and the value of your holding does not change.
What sets the price

In the short run, price is set by supply and demand among traders, and it moves with news, mood and rumour. In the long run, it tends to follow the profits the business produces. A share is worth the cash it will return to its owners over its life, adjusted for the wait and the uncertainty. Since the future is unknown, investors disagree, and the price at any moment is the point where buyers and sellers balance.
Earnings and the multiple

A common yardstick compares the share price with the company's profit per share. A stock priced at 60 dollars with annual earnings of 3 dollars per share trades at 20 times earnings. A high multiple means investors expect profits to grow strongly and are paying in advance for that growth. A low one means they expect little, or see serious risk. The multiple is where the argument about a stock starts, not where it ends.
Risk and reward

Shareholders stand last in line. If a company fails, lenders and suppliers are paid first, and owners usually receive nothing. In exchange for that risk, shareholders keep everything that is left after the fixed claims are met, with no upper limit. Over the past century, broad baskets of American shares have returned on the order of 10 percent a year before inflation, far more than bonds or cash, with severe falls along the way.
Think like an owner

The most useful habit is to remember what you hold. When you buy a share, you are buying part of a business from someone who has decided to sell it. Ask what the business does, how it makes money, whether its profits are likely to be larger in ten years and what you are paying for them. People who treat shares as numbers to be traded tend to do worse than those who treat them as ownership of something real.
Think in fractions of the pot

Poker bets are measured against the pot, not in dollars. A 50 dollar bet is tiny into a pot of 400 and enormous into a pot of 30. Players describe sizes as a third of the pot, half, two thirds, the full pot or an overbet. Thinking this way makes your decisions consistent across stakes and lets you connect the size directly to the odds you are offering your opponent, which is what a bet size really is.
Size by board, not by hand

The worst habit in sizing is betting big with strong hands and small with weak ones, or the reverse. Observant opponents decode it within an hour. The remedy is to choose the size according to the situation, mainly the texture of the board, and use that same size with both your value hands and your bluffs. Then the amount gives nothing away. Your opponent knows what kind of board it is but not which part of your range you hold.
Small on dry boards

On dry flops where you hold the range advantage, small bets of a quarter to a third of the pot are efficient. There are no draws to charge, the opponent must still fold their many missed hands, and when you are behind you lose little. A small bet with a wide range puts the opponent in an awkward spot with all of their weak holdings. This approach is one of the clearest lessons to come out of computer analysis of the game.
Larger on wet boards

When the board is full of draws, your strong hands are vulnerable and your opponent has many hands willing to call. Bet larger, two thirds of the pot or more. This charges draws a price that is wrong for them and builds the pot while you are ahead. A flush draw facing a bet of a third of the pot is delighted. Facing three quarters of the pot with one card to come, it is making a mistake by calling.
Planning three streets

Pots grow geometrically. If you bet the full pot on the flop, turn and river and are called each time, the pot becomes 3 times, then 9 times, then 27 times its starting size, and each player has put in 13 times the original pot. With bets of half the pot, the final pot is only 8 times the start. So with a strong hand and deep stacks, you must begin betting on the flop. You cannot get a whole stack in from the river alone.
Overbets

A bet larger than the pot is an overbet. It is appropriate when you can hold the very strongest hands and your opponent's range is capped, meaning their earlier play has made it unlikely they hold anything huge. The big bet gets maximum value from your monsters and puts maximum pressure on their medium hands. It must be accompanied by some bluffs at the same size. Used only with the nuts, it quickly stops getting paid.
Bluffs follow the same sizes

The size of a bluff determines how often it has to work. A bluff of a third of the pot must succeed one time in four. Half the pot, one in three. The full pot, one in two. A larger bluff forces more folds but costs more when it fails. The right size is the one your value hands would use in the same spot, because a bluff is only believable if it looks the same as the real thing.
Against weaker players

Everything above assumes an opponent who is paying attention. Against players who are not, simplify. If someone calls any bet with any pair, bet your strong hands as large as they will call and do not bluff. If someone folds to every large bet, bluff large and bet small for value. Balanced sizing protects you against experts. Against everyone else, the most profitable size is the one that takes advantage of the specific mistake they keep making.
The boom

The 1920s were prosperous in the United States. Electricity, cars and radios spread into ordinary homes. Share prices rose year after year, and by the late 1920s a growing number of people were buying stocks with borrowed money. An investor could put down as little as a tenth of the price and borrow the rest from a broker, using the shares as security. That worked splendidly while prices climbed. The Dow Jones index reached its peak in early September 1929.
The crash

Prices slid through September and October. On Thursday, October 24, panic selling began. Bankers pooled money to steady the market, and it held for a few days. Then on Monday, October 28, the index fell about 13 percent, and on Tuesday, October 29, about 12 percent more. Investors who had borrowed were forced to sell to repay their loans, which pushed prices down further and forced more selling. Fortunes disappeared in a week.
The long slide

The October crash was only the beginning. After a partial recovery in early 1930, the market fell for more than two years. By its low point in the summer of 1932, the Dow had lost close to 90 percent of its value from the 1929 peak. It did not return to that peak until 1954, a quarter of a century later. Someone who bought at the top and held on waited most of a working lifetime to break even.
From crash to depression

Relatively few Americans owned shares in 1929, so the crash itself touched a minority. The broader damage came through other channels. Confidence collapsed and spending fell. Businesses cut production and laid off workers, who then spent less. The crucial blow was to the banks. Thousands failed between 1930 and 1933. There was no deposit insurance, so when a bank closed, its customers' savings were gone, and fear of that set off runs on healthy banks too.
How bad it got

By 1933, about a quarter of the American workforce was unemployed. Economic output had fallen by more than a quarter. Prices fell steeply, which made debts harder to repay and bankrupted farmers and firms. Breadlines and shanty towns appeared in major cities. The slump spread across the world through trade and finance, and its political consequences in Europe, above all in Germany, were catastrophic.
What went wrong in policy

Economists now largely agree that policy mistakes turned a severe recession into a catastrophe. The Federal Reserve allowed the supply of money to shrink by about a third as banks failed, when it could have supported them. Governments clung to the gold standard, which tied their hands. In 1930 the United States sharply raised tariffs on imports, other countries retaliated, and world trade shrank. Each measure made the contraction deeper.
The reforms

The crisis produced institutions that still exist. From 1933, the federal government insured bank deposits, which largely ended bank runs. A new agency was created in 1934 to regulate the securities markets and require companies to disclose accurate information. Rules limited how much investors could borrow to buy shares. The United States left the gold standard in stages, and recovery began in the countries that abandoned it earliest.
The lessons that were applied

The central lessons were that financial panics feed on themselves and that central banks must act as lenders when everyone else is pulling back. When a severe financial crisis struck in 2008, the people in charge had studied the 1930s closely and responded by flooding the system with money and supporting banks. The downturn was painful, yet unemployment in the United States peaked at about 10 percent, not 25. The memory of 1929 had been put to use.
A map, not a photograph

A schematic shows which parts are connected to which. It deliberately says nothing about where those parts sit on a board or how long the wires are. Two symbols drawn side by side may be at opposite ends of the physical device. That freedom is what makes schematics readable. The designer arranges the symbols to make the logic of the circuit clear, and a separate drawing, the board layout, deals with physical placement.
The common symbols

A resistor is a zigzag line in American drawings and a small rectangle in European ones. A capacitor is two parallel lines, with one curved or marked with a plus sign if it is polarized. An inductor is a row of loops. A diode is a triangle pointing at a bar. A transistor is a circle or bare lines with three leads, one carrying an arrow. Chips are drawn as boxes with numbered pins. There are perhaps twenty symbols you need to recognize at sight.
Lines, dots and crossings

A line is a wire, or more precisely an electrical connection. Where two lines meet and are joined, a dot marks the junction. Where two lines cross without a dot, they are not connected. Good drawings avoid four-way junctions entirely because a missing or smudged dot changes the meaning. If you see lines crossing and cannot tell whether they join, look for the dot. No dot means they simply pass over each other.
Labels instead of wires

On anything but the simplest circuit, drawing every wire would produce a tangle. So designers use labels. Two wire ends carrying the same name, such as RESET or SDA, are connected, even if they are on different pages. Power and ground get their own symbols. Ground is usually a small triangle or a set of three shrinking horizontal lines. Supply rails appear as an arrow or bar with a name such as 5V or VCC. Every identical symbol is the same connection.
Reference designators

Each part carries a short code. R is a resistor, C a capacitor, L an inductor, D a diode, Q a transistor, U a chip, J a connector, SW a switch and F a fuse. The number after the letter identifies the individual part: R1, R2, C7. The same code is printed on the circuit board beside the part, which is how you get from the diagram to the physical component. Beside each designator is the part's value or type number.
The usual layout

Schematics follow reading conventions. Signals generally flow from left to right, with inputs on the left and outputs on the right. Higher voltages are drawn toward the top of the page and ground toward the bottom, so current flows downward. Large designs are split into functional blocks, such as power supply, processor and audio output, often one per page. Knowing these habits lets you orient yourself in an unfamiliar diagram within seconds.
How to approach a new one

Start with the power. Find where it enters, what regulates it and which voltages are produced. Next find the main chips and look up what each one does. Then trace a single signal from input to output, one stage at a time, asking what each part contributes. Do not try to absorb the whole sheet at once. Most circuits are a chain of familiar building blocks: a divider here, a filter there, a transistor switch at the end.
Drawing your own

When you design or modify a circuit, draw it before you build it. Free programs such as KiCad let you place symbols, wire them and check for errors such as unconnected pins. Keep the drawing tidy, label every signal that leaves a block, and write values beside every part. A clear schematic is the single best aid when something does not work, and it is the document you will thank yourself for six months later when you have forgotten how the thing was wired.
Is it the battery

The classic signs of a flat battery are a rapid clicking when you turn the key, an engine that turns over slowly and gives up, or no response at all with the dashboard lights dim or dead. If the lights are bright and the engine cranks strongly but will not fire, the battery is probably not the problem and a jump will not help. Interior lights left on, short trips in cold weather and an ageing battery are the usual causes.
Before you connect anything

Check your owner's manual first, since some cars have special jump-start terminals under the bonnet instead of at the battery, and hybrids and electric cars have their own rules. Do not attempt to jump a battery that is cracked, leaking or frozen. Park the working car close without the two vehicles touching. Switch off both engines and all accessories, set the parking brakes and put both cars in park or neutral.
The four connections

Jump leads have a red pair of clamps and a black pair. Connect in this order. First, a red clamp to the positive terminal of the flat battery, marked with a plus sign. Second, the other red clamp to the positive terminal of the good battery. Third, a black clamp to the negative terminal of the good battery. Fourth, the last black clamp to a bare, unpainted metal part of the engine or frame of the car with the flat battery, away from the battery itself.
Why the last clamp goes on metal

The final connection completes the circuit and often makes a small spark. A battery being charged can give off hydrogen gas, which is flammable. Making that last connection on a solid metal part some distance from the battery keeps any spark away from the gas. It is a small precaution with a real purpose, and it is the step most often skipped. Keep the clamps from touching each other once any of them is connected.
Starting

Start the engine of the working car and let it run for a few minutes to put some charge into the flat battery. Then try to start the other car. If it does not catch, wait a few more minutes and try again. Do not crank for more than a few seconds at a time. If it refuses after several attempts, the battery may be beyond recovery, or the fault lies elsewhere, such as the starter motor or a bad connection.
Disconnecting

Once the car is running, remove the leads in the reverse order: black from the metal ground, black from the good battery, red from the good battery, red from the revived one. Keep the clamps apart as you go. Then drive the revived car for at least twenty to thirty minutes so that the alternator can recharge the battery. Short trips will not do it, and the car may fail to start again next time.
Afterwards

A battery that went flat because a light was left on will usually recover fully. One that went flat for no clear reason is probably near the end of its life, especially if it is more than four years old. Have it tested. If a fairly new battery keeps going flat, the charging system or a hidden electrical drain may be responsible, and a garage can measure both quickly.
The portable alternative

Compact lithium jump starters, about the size of a paperback book, have largely removed the need for a second car. You connect the unit's clamps to the battery, wait a moment and start the engine. They hold their charge for months, though they should be topped up a few times a year, and most also charge phones. For anyone who drives alone or in remote places, keeping one in the boot is inexpensive insurance.
The replication crisis

A scientific finding is supposed to be repeatable. If another team runs the same experiment, they should get the same result. In 2015 a large collaboration of researchers repeated 100 studies that had been published in leading psychology journals. Only a little over a third produced a clear result the second time, and the effects were on average about half the original size. Similar problems have since been found in parts of medicine and economics.
Why it happened

Most of this was not fraud. Journals preferred surprising positive results, so studies that found nothing went unpublished. Samples were often small, which makes flukes more likely. Researchers had many choices about which data to include and which comparisons to run, and could try several until one produced a publishable result, frequently without realizing what they were doing. A field can generate a large body of false findings this way while everyone acts in good faith.
Willpower as a fuel tank

One influential idea, called ego depletion, held that self-control draws on a limited resource that runs down with use. In the original 1998 experiment, people who resisted eating chocolate gave up sooner on a later puzzle. Hundreds of studies followed. In 2016, a coordinated attempt across 23 laboratories and more than two thousand participants found an effect close to zero. The idea that willpower is depleted like a battery is now regarded as doubtful at best.
Power posing

A 2010 study reported that standing in an expansive posture for two minutes raised testosterone, lowered a stress hormone and made people take more risks. The idea reached an enormous audience. A larger repetition in 2015 found no hormonal or behavioural effects, and one of the original authors publicly stated that she no longer believed the effects were real. People may report feeling more confident after such poses. The physiological claims have not held up.
The marshmallow test

In studies begun in the 1960s, young children were offered one treat now or two if they could wait. Later follow-ups reported that those who waited did better in school and in life, and the test became a symbol of the importance of self-control. A 2018 study with a much larger and more varied sample found the link was far weaker and mostly disappeared once family background was taken into account. A child's ability to wait reflected their circumstances as much as their character.
Others under question

The list goes on. Claims that reading words related to old age makes people walk more slowly have failed to repeat. The effect of holding a pen in the mouth to force a smile turned out to be much smaller than first reported. The Stanford prison experiment of 1971 has been heavily criticized after evidence emerged that the guards were coached. Not every challenged finding is false, but each of these deserves much less confidence than its fame suggests.
What did hold up

Many classic findings have survived repeated testing. Anchoring is robust. So is the tendency to recall material better after testing than after rereading, and the benefit of spacing study over time. The Stroop effect, in which naming the ink colour of a colour word is slowed when the two conflict, is among the most reliable in the field. The crisis did not show that psychology is worthless. It showed which parts rest on firm ground.
How to read a headline

The field has responded with larger samples, plans registered before data are collected and routine replication. For a reader, a few questions help. Was the study large? Has anyone repeated it? Is the claimed effect surprisingly big for such a small intervention? Is one study being presented as settled fact? A single exciting result is a suggestion. A finding repeated by independent teams is knowledge. Popular science books written before about 2015 should be read with that in mind.
A tradable loan

When a government or company wants to borrow, it can issue bonds. The buyer of a bond is lending money. In return, the issuer promises to pay a fixed amount of interest, called the coupon, at regular intervals, and to repay the original amount, the face value, on a set date, the maturity. A bond with a face value of 1,000 dollars and a 4 percent coupon pays 40 dollars a year until it matures, then returns the 1,000.
Why the price changes

Bonds can be sold to other investors before they mature, and the price is whatever a buyer will pay. Suppose you hold that 4 percent bond and interest rates rise, so that new bonds pay 5 percent. Nobody will pay 1,000 dollars for your 40 dollars a year when the same money now buys 50. To sell, you must drop the price until your bond's return matches the new rate. The payments have not changed. The bond's market value has fallen.
The seesaw

This is the central rule. When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall. When rates fall, existing bonds become more valuable, because they pay more than new ones, and their prices rise. The two always move in opposite directions. If you hold a bond to maturity and the issuer pays, you receive exactly what was promised, and the price changes along the way do not matter to you. They matter if you need to sell early.
Yield

A bond's yield is the return a buyer earns at the current price. If the 4 percent bond can be bought for 920 dollars, the buyer collects 40 dollars a year on an outlay of 920, plus an 80 dollar gain when 1,000 is repaid at maturity. The yield is therefore higher than 4 percent. Price down means yield up. News reports saying that bond yields rose are describing a fall in bond prices.
Longer bonds swing more

The further away a bond's maturity, the more its price reacts to a change in rates. A bond with one year left will soon be repaid and reinvested at the new rate, so its price barely moves. A bond with thirty years left locks its owner into the old rate for decades. As a rough guide, a ten-year bond loses something like 8 percent of its value when rates rise by one percentage point. Investors call this sensitivity duration.
Will you be repaid

The second risk is default. A government that borrows in its own currency is very unlikely to fail to pay, so its bonds offer the lowest yields. Companies can and do go bankrupt, so their bonds must pay more to attract lenders. Rating agencies grade issuers from the highest quality down to speculative, often called junk. The extra yield on a risky bond is compensation for the chance of loss. It is not free income.
The yield curve

Plot the yields of government bonds against their maturities and you get the yield curve. Normally it slopes upward, since lenders want more for tying money up longer. Occasionally short-term yields rise above long-term ones, and the curve is said to be inverted. In the United States, such inversions have preceded most recessions of recent decades, which is why the shape gets so much attention, though the timing has varied widely.
Why hold them

Bonds provide steadier returns than shares and predictable income, and high-quality ones have often held their value when shares fell. They are not risk-free in the short run. In 2022, when central banks raised rates rapidly, broad American bond indexes fell by more than a tenth, their worst year in generations. The basic trade remains. Lending is safer than owning, pays less over time, and is sensitive to the path of interest rates.
Where the profit comes from

Bluffs are memorable, but most of a winning player's income is value: betting the best hand and having a worse one call. At low and middle stakes, where opponents call too often, this is overwhelmingly true. A player who never bluffed but extracted full value from every strong hand would beat most casual games comfortably. A player who bluffs brilliantly but checks back winning hands on the river leaves money behind every session.
The test

A value bet is correct when, among the hands that will call you, more than half are worse than yours. The question to ask before betting is concrete: which worse hands call this bet? If you can name several likely holdings that are behind you and would pay, bet. If the only hands that call are ones that beat you, the bet achieves nothing. Worse hands fold, better hands call, and you lose the most when you lose.
Thin value

The skill that separates good players from average ones is betting hands that are only modestly strong. This is called thin value. Top pair with a middling kicker on the river, or second pair against an opponent who called twice with what looks like a draw that missed and a pair that did not. Average players check these hands, glad to reach showdown. Strong players bet a small amount and are called by weaker pairs often enough to profit.
Why players miss it

The barrier is fear. Betting a medium hand feels risky because sometimes you will be raised or shown a better hand, and those moments are vivid. The many times a worse hand quietly calls a small bet are less memorable. It helps to accept in advance that a correct thin value bet will run into a better hand a fair share of the time. If you are never called by better when you bet the river, you are not betting enough hands.
Size to the caller

The right amount is the largest your opponent's worse hands will pay. Against someone who hates folding any pair, bet big with strong hands, since the size barely affects whether they call. Against a cautious player, a smaller bet is called far more often and earns more on average. Think about what specific hands you are targeting. If you want a call from a weak top pair, do not bet an amount that only two pair would consider.
Do not slow play by default

Checking a strong hand to trap is tempting and usually costs money. It gives free cards to hands that could beat you, and it fails to build a pot. A big hand wants a big pot, and pots are built by betting on every street. Slow playing has a place on very dry boards against aggressive opponents who will bet if you check. Against passive players who call but rarely bet, checking a strong hand just means winning less.
The river check behind

The opposite error is betting a hand that cannot be called by worse. On the river with a medium-strength hand in position, such as a weak pair when the draws have missed, ask the test question honestly. If your opponent's worse hands are busted draws that will fold, and their better hands will call, then check and take the showdown. Betting there turns a hand with real value into a bluff that only gets called when it loses.
A session drill

For one session, at every river where you hold a made hand and it is your turn to bet, silently name three worse hands that would call. If you can, bet. If you cannot, check. Afterwards, note the hands where you checked and won against something that would have paid. Those are your missed bets. Most players find several a night, and adding them back is one of the quickest ways to raise a win rate.
A discovery in Berlin

At the end of 1938, chemists in Berlin found that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced a much lighter element. The physicist Lise Meitner, who had fled Nazi Germany, and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out what it meant. The uranium nucleus had split in two, releasing a large amount of energy. Physicists quickly realized that each split also released neutrons that could split further nuclei. A chain reaction, and with it a bomb of unprecedented power, was possible in principle.
The letter

Refugee scientists in America feared that Germany would get there first. In August 1939, the Hungarian physicist Leo Szilard persuaded Albert Einstein to sign a letter to President Franklin Roosevelt warning of the danger and urging American research. The response was slow at first. After the United States entered the war, the effort became a crash programme. In 1942 it was placed under the Army, commanded by General Leslie Groves and code-named the Manhattan Project.
The first reactor

On December 2, 1942, in a squash court beneath a stadium at the University of Chicago, a team led by the Italian physicist Enrico Fermi achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. Their reactor was a stack of graphite blocks and uranium, with control rods to stop it. It ran for a few minutes at a tiny power level. It proved that a chain reaction could be started and controlled, the essential step toward both bombs and nuclear power.
An industrial effort

The hard part was producing the material. A bomb needed either a rare form of uranium, which had to be separated atom by atom from the common form, or plutonium, a new element made in reactors. Enormous plants were built at Oak Ridge in Tennessee and Hanford in Washington state. The bomb itself was designed at Los Alamos in New Mexico under the physicist Robert Oppenheimer. At its height the project employed well over a hundred thousand people and cost about two billion dollars.
Trinity

Two designs emerged. The uranium bomb was simple enough that it was never tested. The plutonium bomb required a difficult arrangement of explosives to squeeze a sphere of metal inward, and it had to be tried. On July 16, 1945, in the New Mexico desert, the test code-named Trinity released the energy of roughly twenty thousand tons of conventional explosive. Germany had surrendered two months earlier. The war with Japan continued.
Hiroshima and Nagasaki

On August 6, 1945, an American bomber dropped the uranium bomb on the city of Hiroshima. Three days later, a plutonium bomb was dropped on Nagasaki. Estimates of the dead by the end of that year are around 140,000 in Hiroshima and 70,000 in Nagasaki, most of them civilians, with more dying later from injuries and radiation. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan between the two bombings. Japan announced its surrender on August 15.
The argument that has not ended

Whether the bombs should have been used has been debated ever since. Defenders argue that they ended the war quickly and avoided an invasion of Japan that would have cost very many lives on both sides. Critics argue that Japan was close to surrender, that the Soviet entry into the war was decisive, or that a demonstration should have been attempted first. Historians continue to disagree, and the surviving evidence supports more than one reading.
What it began

The American monopoly lasted four years. The Soviet Union tested its own bomb in 1949, helped by information from spies inside the project. The arms race that followed produced tens of thousands of far more powerful weapons. The project also created the model of science organized on an industrial scale with government money, and it left many of its own scientists campaigning for control of what they had built. The questions it raised, about who should hold such weapons and how to prevent their use, have been part of world politics ever since.
What a datasheet is

A datasheet is the manufacturer's official description of a component. It states what the part does, how to connect it, what it can tolerate and how it performs. Datasheets are free, and you find one by searching for the part number printed on the component. They range from two pages for a resistor to hundreds for a microcontroller. Nobody reads them from beginning to end. The skill is knowing where to look.
The first page

Page one is a summary written partly by the marketing department. It gives a one-paragraph description, a list of headline features and typical applications. This is enough to decide whether the part is even a candidate. Treat the numbers here with caution. The headline figure is usually the best case under ideal conditions. The figures you can rely on are in the tables further in, with the test conditions spelled out.
Absolute maximum ratings

This table lists the limits beyond which the part may be permanently damaged: the highest supply voltage, the highest voltage on any pin, the most current, the temperature range. These are not operating conditions. A part run at its absolute maximum may survive, but nothing about its performance is promised, and its life is shortened. Find this table before you connect power to anything. It tells you which mistakes are fatal.
Recommended operating conditions

The next table gives the range in which the part is designed to work properly. A chip might have an absolute maximum supply of 6 volts and a recommended range of 2.7 to 5.5. Design to stay inside the recommended range under all circumstances, including a fresh battery, a hot day and a noisy supply. The gap between the recommended and absolute figures is a safety margin for accidents, not extra room for the design.
Minimum, typical, maximum

The electrical characteristics tables usually have three columns. The typical value is what an average part does at room temperature. It is not guaranteed. The minimum and maximum columns are what the manufacturer promises for every part across the stated conditions. A design that only works with typical values will fail on some units. Always design to the worst-case column that applies, and read the footnotes giving the conditions under which each figure was measured.
Pinout and package

The pin diagram shows which pin is which, viewed from the top unless stated otherwise. Pin 1 is marked on the physical part by a dot, a notch or a bevelled corner. The same chip often comes in several packages with different pin arrangements, so check that the diagram matches the version you hold. A table lists each pin's name and function. Getting the pinout wrong is the most common way to destroy a part on first power-up.
The graphs

Further in are charts showing how performance changes with temperature, voltage, current and frequency. These answer the questions the tables cannot. How much does the output voltage drop as the load increases? How does an LED's brightness vary with current? How much does a battery's capacity fall in the cold? When your operating point differs from the single test condition in the table, the graphs are where the real answer lives.
The application circuit

Most datasheets for chips include a typical application circuit: a complete, working schematic with component values. This is the manufacturer showing you how they expect the part to be used. Start from it. Copy the recommended values and, for power and radio parts especially, follow the layout advice. A great many problems in hobby and professional designs alike come from departing from the reference circuit without a good reason.
What it is

A check-raise is exactly what the name says. You check, your opponent bets, and you raise. It was once considered so underhanded that some card rooms banned it. Today it is standard and essential. The player who acts first is at a disadvantage on every street. The check-raise is the tool that offsets it, because it allows the first player to trap bets that the second player makes simply because they were checked to.
Why not just bet

When you are out of position against the player who raised before the flop, that player will bet a large share of flops whatever they hold. If you bet first with a strong hand, they fold their misses and you win a small pot. If you check, they bet their misses, and now your raise captures that extra money. Checking lets them put chips in with hands that would never have called a bet. The check-raise wins bigger pots with the same cards.
For value

The foundation is strong hands: two pair, sets, and top pair with a good kicker on boards where opponents will continue with worse. On wet boards, raising also charges the many draws that would otherwise see the next card cheaply. Size the raise to about three times your opponent's bet, somewhat more if you will be out of position for the rest of the hand and the board is full of draws. A tiny raise gives every draw the right price.
As a semi-bluff

If you only check-raise strong hands, attentive opponents will fold whenever you do it. So add draws. A flush draw, an open-ended straight draw, or a gutshot with two overcards all make good candidates. These hands can win immediately when the opponent folds, and they can still win by improving when called. A draw played this way earns far more than a draw played by calling and hoping, because it has two ways to succeed.
Choosing the board

The play works best on flops that favour the caller's range: low and middling connected boards such as seven, six, four or eight, five, three. The preflop raiser's big cards have mostly missed, and you can credibly hold two pair, sets and straights. On boards with an ace or king, the raiser's range is strong and yours is not, so check-raising as a bluff there is expensive. Match the play to boards where the strong hands are plausibly yours.
Against the right player

Check-raising needs an opponent who bets when checked to. Against someone who makes a continuation bet on nearly every flop, it is very profitable, as their betting range is full of air. Against a passive player who only bets strong hands, checking a big hand risks giving a free card, so simply bet. And if a tight, passive player check-raises you, believe them. At low stakes, that line is a strong hand far more often than not.
After you raise

Have a plan for the turn. If called, your opponent usually has a pair or a draw. With a strong made hand, keep betting, sized to the wetness of the board. With a semi-bluff, continue on cards that improve your hand or that are bad for your opponent's likely holdings, and be willing to give up on blanks. The mistake to avoid is automatic follow-through. A second and third bet with nothing must have a reason behind it.
Defending against it

When you are the one check-raised, the answer depends on who did it and on what board. Against aggressive players on draw-heavy boards, continue with your good pairs and your own draws, since they are bluffing some of the time. Against passive players, fold all but your strongest hands. You can also reduce your exposure in advance by checking back some flops, which removes the weak bets that a check-raise feeds on.
What it draws

An oscilloscope plots voltage against time. The vertical axis is voltage and the horizontal axis is time, sweeping from left to right. A steady DC voltage appears as a flat horizontal line. A signal that varies shows its shape: a smooth sine wave, the square edges of a digital signal, a brief spike. A meter would average all of that into a single reading. The scope shows what is actually happening, which is often the only way to find a fault.
The two main knobs

Two controls set the view. The vertical scale, in volts per division, sets how many volts each grid square represents. The horizontal scale, in time per division, sets how much time each square covers. Adjust them until the signal fills a good part of the screen and a few cycles are visible. Most digital scopes have an auto-set button that makes a reasonable first attempt, which is a fine place to start before adjusting by hand.
The trigger

Without a trigger, a repeating signal would be redrawn at random starting points and smear across the screen. The trigger tells the scope to start each sweep at the same point on the waveform, typically when the voltage crosses a chosen level while rising. The picture then stands still. For a signal that happens only once, single-shot triggering waits for the event and freezes it. Learning to set the trigger is the step that makes a scope useful.
Probes

The probe is part of the measurement. Standard probes have a switch for times one and times ten. In the times ten position, the signal is reduced tenfold and the probe presents ten times more resistance and less capacitance to the circuit, disturbing it less. Use times ten by default. Each probe also has a small trimmer that should be adjusted, using the square-wave test terminal on the scope, until the edges of the square look clean and flat.
Bandwidth

Every scope has a bandwidth rating in megahertz. At that frequency, a sine wave is already displayed at only about 70 percent of its true height. Digital signals contain frequencies far above their basic rate, in the sharp edges. A common rule is to choose a scope with a bandwidth at least five times the highest frequency you care about. For audio and most microcontroller work, an entry-level instrument of 50 to 100 megahertz is ample.
The ground clip warning

The ground clip on a probe is connected, through the scope's chassis, to the earth pin of its mains plug. It is not a floating reference like the black lead of a battery multimeter. If you clip it to a point in a mains-powered circuit that is not at earth potential, you create a short circuit through the scope. For battery-powered and low-voltage projects, clipping to circuit ground is fine. Do not probe mains circuits without proper training and isolation.
What it reveals

Many faults are invisible to a meter and obvious on a scope. Noise riding on a power rail that resets a microcontroller. A button that produces a dozen pulses when pressed once. A data line with slow, rounded edges. A regulator that oscillates. A signal that arrives at the right voltage but the wrong time. Seeing the shape tells you what kind of problem you have, and half of fixing a circuit is knowing that.
Getting one

Scopes used to cost as much as a car. A capable four-channel digital bench scope is now within the budget of a keen hobbyist, and pocket-sized or USB instruments cost far less, with limits on speed. For serial data, an inexpensive logic analyser that decodes the bits is often a better tool. If you are deciding whether you need a scope, the usual sign is that you have started guessing at what a signal is doing.
Why bluff at all

If you only bet with strong hands, observant opponents stop paying you. They fold when you bet and take the pot when you check. Bluffing is what forces them to call your value bets. In theory, the right mix of bluffs and value hands leaves your opponent with no profitable response. In practice, at most tables, bluffing is a tool to use selectively against players who fold too much and to put away against players who do not.
The ratio on the river

On the last street there is a clean relationship between bet size and how many bluffs you can include. When you bet the size of the pot, your opponent is getting 2 to 1 and needs to win a third of the time. So a balanced betting range has one bluff for every two value hands. With a bet of half the pot, the opponent gets 3 to 1, and the mix is one bluff for every three value hands. Bigger bets permit more bluffs.
Pick hands that cannot win otherwise

The best hands to bluff with are those with no chance at showdown. A missed draw that has become nine high cannot win by checking, so it loses nothing by bluffing. A hand such as third pair might win if checked, so turning it into a bluff wastes that value. This is the first filter. When choosing which of your weak hands to bet, start with the ones that are worthless if you check.
Blockers

The second filter is which cards you hold. If the board shows three spades and you hold the ace of spades with no flush, your opponent cannot have the best possible flush. That makes strong hands less likely in their range and folds more likely. A card that removes combinations of the hands you fear is a blocker. Good river bluffs block the hands that would call. Equally, avoid holding cards that block the missed draws your opponent would fold.
Tell a consistent story

A bluff must represent a specific strong hand, and your actions on earlier streets must fit it. If you called the flop and turn on a board with a flush draw and then bet big when the third suited card arrives, the story makes sense. If you checked twice and then bet big on a harmless river card, it does not. Before bluffing, ask what hand you are claiming to hold and whether you would have played that hand this way.
Bluff on early streets with equity

On the flop and turn, the best bluffs are semi-bluffs: draws and hands with overcards that can improve. They win when the opponent folds and still have a chance when called. Pure bluffs with no possibility of improving are better saved for the river, when all the cards are out. A sensible pattern is to bet many draws on the flop, continue with the better ones on the turn, and on the river bluff with those that missed.
Count the opponents

Each additional player in the pot makes a bluff less likely to work, since every one of them has to fold. A bluff that succeeds 50 percent of the time against one opponent might succeed 25 percent of the time against two with similar tendencies. Bluff mainly in pots with a single opponent. Against several, bet your real hands and your strong draws and let the rest go.
Most games are under-bluffed

All of this theory assumes an opponent who can fold. Many recreational players call far too often, driven by curiosity and by the fear of being bluffed. Against them, the right number of bluffs is close to zero, and the right response is to bet your good hands larger. The reverse also holds. At lower stakes, big bets and raises on the river are strong hands far more often than theory would predict. When a quiet player suddenly bets big, folding is usually right.
Look before you measure

Start with your eyes and nose, with the power off. Look for a part in backwards, a wire in the wrong hole, a solder bridge between two pins, a joint that never flowed, a component missing entirely. Look for scorch marks, bulging capacitors and cracked parts. Smell for the sharp odour of burnt electronics. Compare the build against the schematic, one connection at a time. A large share of faults are found at this stage without any instrument.
Power first, always

If nothing obvious appears, apply power and measure the supply. Is the voltage present at the input? Is it present after the regulator, and is it the right value? Is it present at the power pin of every chip, measured at the pin itself and not at the supply? Is ground really connected everywhere? Experienced technicians check power first every time, because a missing or sagging supply produces symptoms that look like a dozen other faults.
Feel for heat

With the circuit powered, carefully check for anything getting hot. A chip or regulator that is too hot to keep a finger on is usually being asked for too much current, often because of a short downstream or a part fitted backwards. Use the back of a finger and be cautious, since a shorted part can burn. A part that should be warm and is stone cold is also information: it may not be getting power at all.
Split the circuit in half

For a circuit with several stages, do not check them in order. Check the middle. If the signal is correct at the midpoint, the fault lies in the second half. If not, it is in the first. Then split the faulty half again. This approach finds a fault in a chain of sixteen stages in four measurements. It is the same strategy as looking up a word in a dictionary by opening it in the middle.
Know what you expect

A measurement is only useful if you have a prediction to compare it with. Before touching the probe to a point, decide what the voltage should be there and why. If the reading matches, move on. If it does not, you have found something. People who probe without expectations collect numbers and learn nothing. Working out what each point ought to read is also how you come to understand the circuit properly.
Change one thing at a time

When you think you have found the cause, make one change and test. If you change three things and the circuit starts working, you do not know which mattered, and if it gets worse, you do not know which to undo. Keep notes of what you measured and what you changed. Twenty minutes into a difficult fault, it is easy to forget which combinations have been tried, and you start repeating yourself.
Suspect your assumptions

The hardest faults are the ones where something you were sure about is wrong. The new part is faulty. The wire you trust is broken inside its insulation. The chip is a different version with a different pinout. The supply is fine at rest and collapses under load. When nothing makes sense, list what you have assumed without checking and test each item. Explaining the problem aloud to someone else, or to nobody, often exposes the hidden assumption.
The usual suspects

Faults cluster. In new builds: wiring errors, reversed parts, bad solder joints, missing ground connections and wrong values. In old equipment: dried-out capacitors, cracked solder joints near connectors and anything that gets hot, corroded contacts and worn switches. In anything with a microcontroller: the code. Before concluding that you have found a rare and interesting failure, rule out the common dull ones. They are the cause nearly every time.
The mistake of putting someone on a hand

Beginners decide that an opponent has ace king and then play the rest of the hand as if that were known. Sometimes they are right, which reinforces the habit. More often the opponent turns over something else and the beginner is baffled. Nobody can deduce two exact cards from a few bets. What can be deduced is the collection of hands consistent with what the opponent has done. That collection is called a range.
Start before the flop

A range begins with the first action. A tight player raising from early position might hold big pairs, ace king, ace queen and a few suited big cards, perhaps one hand in eight. A loose player raising on the button might hold four hands in ten. A player who just calls a raise rarely has aces or kings, since most players reraise those. Position, the action and what you know of the player set the starting list.
Narrow with each action

Every later decision removes hands from the list. Suppose the flop is king, eight, three and the raiser bets. That keeps most of the range, since many players bet any two cards here. The turn is a two and they bet again, larger. Now the weakest hands drop out. On the river they bet a third time. By this point, a typical player's range is mostly a king with a good kicker or better, plus an occasional busted bluff.
Weigh, do not eliminate

Ranges are not just in or out. Some hands are more likely than others within the range. A player might bet three streets with ace king every time and with a bluff one time in five. Good hand readers weight the possibilities instead of crossing them off. They also keep unlikely hands in mind for players who have shown they are capable of odd plays. The picture is a set of probabilities that shifts with each bet.
Your own range

The idea applies to you as well. Your opponents, if they are thinking, are assigning you a range. So ask what your line looks like from across the table. If you would only play a hand this way with very strong holdings, your bets will get too many folds, or your checks will invite bluffs. Thinking about your whole range in a spot, not just the hand you happen to hold, is how good players stay hard to read.
Capped and uncapped

A range is capped when it cannot contain the strongest hands. If a player just calls before the flop and then calls bets on a board of ace, king, queen, they are unlikely to hold a set or two pair of the top cards, having not raised at any point. Their range has a ceiling. A capped range is vulnerable to large bets, because its owner can never be confident. Recognizing when an opponent is capped is a signal to apply pressure.
Compare equity against the range

Once you have a range in mind, the decision is arithmetic. How does your hand do against all of it? If the pot is offering 3 to 1 and your hand beats a third of the hands in their range, call. This is far more reliable than fearing the single worst possibility or hoping for the best one. Software lets you practise this away from the table by entering a range and seeing your equity against it.
Building the habit

Start small. On every hand you watch, even those you have folded, guess the raiser's range before the flop and revise it as the action unfolds. When cards are shown, check whether the hand was inside your range. If it was not, ask what you missed. Over a few months, this turns hand reading from a mysterious talent into a routine, and it works equally well against players you have never seen before.
Voltage comes from chemistry

A battery cell produces a voltage set by the materials inside it, not by its size. An alkaline cell gives about 1.5 volts whether it is a small AAA or a large D. A nickel metal hydride rechargeable gives about 1.2. A lithium-ion cell gives a nominal 3.6 or 3.7. A lead-acid cell gives about 2.1, and six in series make the familiar 12 volt car battery. To get more voltage, cells are stacked in series. Size affects only how long the cell lasts.
Capacity

Capacity is measured in amp hours or milliamp hours: current multiplied by time. A good AA alkaline holds roughly 2,000 to 3,000 milliamp hours at low drain. A common cylindrical lithium-ion cell holds 2,500 to 3,500. A coin cell of the CR2032 type holds only about 220. To compare batteries of different voltages fairly, multiply capacity by voltage to get watt hours, which is the stored energy.
Voltage sags as you use it

A battery's voltage is not constant. An alkaline cell starts above 1.5 volts and declines steadily toward 1.0 as it empties, so devices that need a firm 1.5 volts quit while much of the energy remains. Lithium-ion holds a flatter voltage through most of its discharge, from 4.2 volts when full to about 3.0 when empty. This is why a fuel gauge based on voltage alone works tolerably for alkaline cells and poorly for lithium ones.
Internal resistance

Every battery behaves as if it had a small resistor in series with it. When you draw current, some voltage is lost across that internal resistance, and the battery warms. Alkaline cells have fairly high internal resistance, so they perform poorly in high-drain devices such as camera flashes, delivering a fraction of their rated capacity. Rechargeable cells have much lower internal resistance and handle heavy loads far better, despite their lower nominal voltage.
The C rate

Charge and discharge currents are often quoted relative to capacity. A rate of 1C means a current that would empty the battery in one hour. For a 2,000 milliamp hour cell, 1C is 2 amps, and half that rate is 1 amp. Each cell type has limits. Ordinary lithium-ion cells are typically charged at half C to 1C. Cells built for power tools and drones can discharge at 10C or more. Exceeding the rating overheats the cell.
Lithium needs respect

Lithium-ion cells store a great deal of energy in a small space, several times more per kilogram than lead-acid. They must be kept within strict limits. Charged above about 4.2 volts, discharged below about 2.5 to 3, short-circuited or punctured, they can overheat and catch fire. Nearly every pack includes a protection circuit, and they need a charger designed for the chemistry. Do not charge them when they are below freezing. A swollen cell should be retired at once.
Making them last

Rechargeable batteries wear out with use and with time. For lithium-ion, heat is the main enemy, followed by being held at full charge. A laptop kept plugged in at 100 percent in a warm room ages faster than one cycled between 30 and 80 percent. For long storage, leave lithium cells at around half charge in a cool place. Nickel metal hydride cells of the low self-discharge type hold most of their charge for a year on the shelf.
Choosing for a project

For a device that sips power for months, such as a remote control or a clock, alkaline cells are cheap and simple. For anything used daily with moderate drain, low self-discharge nickel metal hydride cells pay for themselves quickly. For compact, high-energy designs, lithium-ion or lithium polymer with a proper charging and protection module is standard. For large amounts of energy where weight does not matter, lead-acid remains cheap and forgiving.
What changes on the river

On earlier streets, hands have potential. Draws can arrive and leads can change. On the river all of that is finished. Your hand's value is fixed, and it will either win at showdown or it will not. There is nothing left to protect against and no equity to deny. The only purposes of a river bet are to get called by a worse hand or to make a better hand fold. A bet that does neither is a mistake.
Three categories

Sort your hand into one of three groups. A value hand is strong enough that worse hands will call a bet. A bluff is a hand that cannot win at showdown and can only take the pot by betting. In between are hands with showdown value: good enough to win sometimes when checked, not good enough to be called by worse. These medium hands should usually check. Betting them drives out everything they beat.
In position

When you act last and are checked to, the decision is simple. With a value hand, bet an amount that worse hands will pay. With a hand that has showdown value, check behind and see who wins. With nothing, decide whether your opponent will fold often enough to justify a bluff, given the size you would need. Acting last means you never face a raise after checking, which is one more reason position is worth so much.
Out of position

First to act is harder. If you check a strong hand hoping to raise, the opponent may check behind and you win nothing extra. If you bet a medium hand, you may be raised off it. A common approach is to bet your strong hands and your chosen bluffs, and to check your medium hands planning to call some bets and fold to others. Against aggressive opponents, checking a few strong hands as well keeps them from attacking every check.
Facing a bet

When your opponent bets the river, work out the price. A bet of half the pot means you need to hold the best hand 25 percent of the time. A pot-sized bet means 33 percent. Then estimate, from the way the hand was played, how often this player is bluffing or betting a worse hand for value. If that is more often than the price requires, call. If less, fold. The strength of your own hand matters only relative to their range.
Bluff catchers

A bluff catcher is a hand that beats every bluff and loses to every value bet. Top pair on a board where a flush and a straight have both arrived is a typical example. With such a hand, raising is pointless, and the choice is call or fold. The useful question is whether there are enough missed draws in the opponent's range. If every obvious draw completed on the river, they have few natural bluffs and you should fold more.
Raises mean strength

A river raise is the strongest action in poker. In most games, particularly at low and middle stakes, players almost never raise the river as a bluff. They raise with the nuts or close to it. Folding a good hand to a river raise feels terrible and is usually correct. Over time, the players who pay off river raises with one pair or two pair, just to see it, give back a large part of what they win elsewhere.
Take your time

The river is where pots are biggest and mistakes cost the most. There is no penalty for pausing. Replay the hand from the start: what the opponent did before the flop, how they reacted to each card, what sizes they used. Ask which hands play this way. Then decide. Many expensive errors on the river are made in two seconds by players who would have got it right with twenty.
Voltages as bits

A digital signal carries information as one of two states, high or low, usually written 1 and 0. Physically, these are voltage ranges. In a 5 volt system, a voltage near 5 is high and near zero is low. In a 3.3 volt system, high is near 3.3. Most modern microcontrollers and sensors use 3.3 volts or lower, because lower voltages save power and suit smaller transistors. Older designs and many hobby boards still use 5.
The thresholds

A chip does not require exactly 5 volts or exactly zero. It has thresholds. For a typical 3.3 volt part, anything above about 2 volts is guaranteed to be read as high and anything below about 0.8 volts as low. Between them lies an undefined band where the result is not promised. The gap between what an output delivers and what an input requires is the noise margin, and it is what makes digital circuits tolerant of interference.
Floating inputs

An input pin connected to nothing is not at zero. It is floating. Modern inputs draw almost no current, so the pin's voltage is set by stray electric fields from nearby wires, the mains and even your hand moving past. It drifts unpredictably between high and low. A circuit with a floating input may work on the bench and fail when you lean over it. Every input must be driven to a defined level at all times.
Pull-up and pull-down resistors

The standard cure is a resistor that gently holds the pin at a known level when nothing else is driving it. A pull-up connects the pin to the supply. A pull-down connects it to ground. A push button then needs only to connect the pin to the opposite level when pressed. The usual value is around 10 kilohms: low enough to hold the pin firmly, high enough that little current is wasted while the button is held.
Built-in pull-ups

Most microcontrollers contain optional pull-up resistors on their input pins, switched on in software. They are typically in the range of 20 to 50 kilohms. Enabling one saves an external part. The consequence is that the logic reads backwards from what beginners expect. With a pull-up, the pin reads high when the button is not pressed and low when it is. This arrangement is called active low and is extremely common.
Mixing 5 and 3.3 volts

Connecting parts that run at different voltages needs care in one direction. A 3.3 volt output driving a 5 volt input often works, since 3.3 volts is above the high threshold of many 5 volt inputs, though not all. A 5 volt output driving a 3.3 volt input can damage it, unless the datasheet states that the pin tolerates 5 volts. In that direction, use a voltage divider for slow signals or a level shifter chip for fast or two-way ones.
Outputs that only pull down

Some outputs are open drain, meaning they can connect the line to ground but cannot drive it high. They rely on a pull-up resistor to bring the line up when released. This allows several devices to share one wire safely, since none can fight another by driving high while it drives low. The I2C bus works this way. If a line of this kind is stuck low or never goes high, a missing pull-up is the first thing to check.
How much a pin can drive

A logic output is a signal source, not a power supply. A typical microcontroller pin can safely source or sink something on the order of 10 to 20 milliamps, with a lower limit on the total across all pins. That is enough for an LED with its resistor and not enough for a motor, a relay coil or a strip of lights. Anything heavier needs a transistor or driver chip between the pin and the load.
What tilt is

Tilt is the deterioration of your play caused by emotion. The term comes from pinball, where shaking the machine in frustration causes it to lock up. In poker it usually means anger after a bad beat leading to reckless aggression, but it takes many forms. A player on tilt knows the right play and makes the wrong one. Nearly all experienced players agree that it costs them more than any gap in their technical knowledge.
The kinds

Tilt is not only fury. There is the urge to win back losses quickly by playing bigger pots with weaker hands. There is entitlement, the feeling that after so many lost coin flips you are owed a win. There is fear, playing too tightly after a big loss to avoid another. There is boredom, entering pots because you have folded for an hour. And there is overconfidence after a hot streak. Each one pushes your play away from what you know is correct.
Why it happens

The brain's response to a painful loss is the same system that handles physical threat. Heart rate rises, attention narrows, and the urge to act immediately becomes strong. Careful reasoning is exactly what that state suppresses. Poker also delivers punishment for correct play on a regular basis, which is unusual. Getting your money in as a four to one favourite and losing happens one time in five, and each time it feels like an injustice.
Know your triggers

Players tilt in their own characteristic ways. For one it is a particular opponent who talks too much. For another it is being bluffed and shown the cards. For another, losing three hands in a row, or being card-dead for an hour, or making one mistake that they then cannot stop replaying. Write yours down. A trigger you have named in advance is much easier to notice in the moment than one that takes you by surprise.
Catch it early

Tilt is far easier to stop at the first sign than at full strength. Early signs are physical and behavioural: a hot face, a tight jaw, faster breathing, acting quickly, saying something sharp, thinking about a previous hand during the current one. When you notice one, take the simplest step available. Sit out a round. Stand up. Take ten slow breaths. The aim is to interrupt the reaction before it reaches your decisions.
Set limits before you play

Rules made in advance work because they do not depend on judgement in the moment. A stop-loss is a commitment to quit after losing a set number of buy-ins, commonly two or three. A time limit serves the same purpose, since tired players tilt more easily. Some players also set a rule to quit after any hand that makes them visibly angry. The right moment to leave is always earlier than it feels.
Quitting is a skill

The session ends when you say it does, and choosing that moment well is as much a part of the game as any bet. Leaving while behind feels like accepting a loss. But the loss has already occurred, and the only question is whether you play your best from here. If the answer is no, further hands cost money on average. There will always be another game tomorrow, and you will arrive at it with your bankroll and judgement intact.
Outside the game

What you bring to the table affects how you play. Sleep, food, alcohol, stress from work or home, and playing with money you cannot afford to lose all make tilt more likely. Players who treat poker seriously look after the ordinary things for that reason. If you find yourself chasing losses repeatedly, or playing to escape other problems, that goes beyond tilt. Gambling support services exist for exactly that, and using one is a sound decision.
A computer in one package

A microcontroller combines a processor, memory for the program, working memory and a set of input and output circuits on a single chip. It is designed to be embedded in a product and do one job indefinitely: run a washing machine, read a thermostat, blink a bike light.
